meta.title: Md. Mahmudul Islam | Project Management | Telecom Digital Delivery
meta.description: Program Management Manager at Banglalink Digital Communications (VEON Group). Ten years delivering telecom, logistics and e-governance programmes under PMO governance.

tagline.normal: I turn ambiguous projects into dated, measurable go-lives.
tagline.zb: Committees talk. I ship. Ten years of go-lives that actually went live.

availability.break: On a break from corporate life

rows.focus: Delivery governance for nationwide digital platforms. I run the machinery between product, IT, commercial and field operations — gate criteria agreed before the gate, UAT discipline, and ExCo reporting that leads with the decision needed.
Scaling e-commerce logistics delivery across the country — building the operational processes that let a parcel reach any thana, and the reporting that told the truth about where it didn't.

E-governance platforms under the Digital Bangladesh programme — including delivery work on EkPay, the centralized citizen-to-government payment platform connecting banks, agents and service providers.

programmes.name: Nationwide door-to-door fulfilment for Banglalink

body.normal: One platform consolidating SIM services, FWA, MNP, transfer of ownership and device ordering with automated rider assignment behind it. I ran delivery governance across product, IT, commercial and field operations, from UAT sign-off through to launch.
body.zb: Five separate services crammed into one platform, launched nationwide without slipping the date. Product, IT, commercial and field ops all pulling in different directions; my job was making them pull in one.

programmes.result: Same-day fulfilment for orders placed before noon, across all 64 districts.

programmes.name: EkPay | Bangladesh's centralized P2G bill payment platform or A2i

body.normal: EkPay is Bangladesh's largest payment aggregator — the A2i initiative to give citizens a single centralized People-to-Government payment platform under the Digital Bangladesh vision. I worked on delivery of a platform connecting 15+ banks, 30+ service providers, 50+ assisted agents and 50,000+ syndicated agents, letting citizens pay any bill from cards, bank accounts or digital credit in one place.
body.zb: Before EkPay: a citizen queued at one office to pay one bill, then queued at another. After: one platform, 15+ banks, 30+ service providers, 50,000+ agents — every government bill payable from a phone. That's what 'Digital Bangladesh' looks like when it ships instead of staying a slogan.

programmes.result: One centralized platform for citizen-to-government payments, spanning 15+ banks and 50,000+ agents nationwide.

programmes.name: MVNO partnership — scope, journeys and regulatory path

body.normal: Built the business scope for a state-operator MVNO partnership: cross-operator after-sales routing, the number-portability journey, and a customer onboarding flow with regulatory validation designed in from the start rather than bolted on afterwards.
body.zb: Regulatory sign-off is where partnerships go to die, so I designed it into the onboarding flow on day one instead of praying for it at the end.

programmes.result: Regulatory checkpoints embedded directly in the onboarding flow.

about.title: The person behind the programmes
about.lead: I'm Mahmudul — a program manager who treats delivery as a discipline, not a personality trait. Ten years, three sectors, one recurring problem: a dozen teams each holding a piece of the truth, and nobody holding the whole picture.

sections.body:
I studied Electrical & Electronic Engineering, which taught me something more useful in delivery than in circuit design: systems fail at the interfaces, not in the middle. Two components can each work perfectly and still bring the whole thing down at the point where they meet.

That is precisely where programmes fail too. Product signs off. IT signs off. Commercial signs off. Then launch week arrives and nobody owns the handover between them. My job, in every role I have held, has been to own those interfaces before they become incidents.

I turn ambiguity into a dated, measurable plan, and then I hold the organisation to it — without pretending a bad week is a good one.

In practice that means RAID discipline that people actually maintain, gate criteria agreed before the gate rather than negotiated at it, UAT sign-off that means something, and executive reporting that leads with the decision needed instead of burying it on slide 34.

E-governance at Synesis IT, where platforms had to work for citizens with no fallback option. Logistics at Paperfly, where a process that fails in a remote thana fails in front of a customer at their doorstep. Telecom at Banglalink, where scale means a small design flaw multiplies across 64 districts before anyone files a ticket.

Different industries, same craft.

principles.title: Bad news travels first
principles.body: A programme is only as healthy as its willingness to report a bad week honestly. Permanently green status is not good news — it is missing information.

principles.title: Measure what stakeholders feel
principles.body: Volume is what your process shows you; time is what people experience. Count the days held, not the tickets closed.

principles.title: Design the constraint in
principles.body: Regulatory validation, field realities and vendor limits belong in the design on day one. Bolted on at the end, they become the reason you miss the date.

principles.title: The ask goes on top
principles.body: Executives need the decision first and the evidence second. If your recommendation is on slide 34, it is not a recommendation.

about.nowBody: Where artificial intelligence genuinely belongs in programme governance — not as a dashboard gimmick, but for the unglamorous work: surfacing risks buried in status reports, spotting where approvals silently stall, and drafting the executive summary nobody has time to write.
